chapter_title: FPGA-Based Signal Processing and Motor Control

screens.title: FPGA-Based Signal Processing and Motor Control
screens.subtitle: High-throughput FIR filters, PWM timing, encoder decoding, and hardware PID loops

narration.text: In this lesson you will explore two of the most demanding real-time FPGA applications: signal processing and motor control. We will make concrete how an FPGA accelerates tasks like a 100-tap FIR filter by implementing multipliers and adders in parallel, and how precise timing for motors—Pulse Width Modulation, encoder counting, and PID loops—benefits from hardware determinism. You will see Verilog patterns: a shift-register delay line for an FIR, parallel multipliers mapped to DSP blocks, a comparator-based PWM generator, and a quadrature decoder that counts edges and direction. For each idea I will give a short Verilog example, a common implementation pitfall to avoid, and a practical verification step you can run in a simulator. You will also get a hands-on activity tying a 16-bit PWM to an LED and reading a potentiometer through an ADC. By the end of this chapter you will understand why FPGAs produce outputs every clock cycle for streaming DSP and why they can run PID loops orders of magnitude faster than a microcontroller. Think about one system you know that requires deterministic responses — how might these techniques improve it?

keyIdea.title: Why FPGAs for DSP & Control
keyIdea.text: FPGAs implement parallel hardware pipelines that give deterministic, sample-rate outputs and low-latency control — ideal for high-speed FIR filters and motor loops.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll master in this chapter

narration.text: These objectives frame the practical skills you'll gain. First, you will implement a Finite Impulse Response filter in Verilog using FPGA DSP resources. That means you will design a delay line, map coefficient multiplies to hardware DSP blocks, and assemble an adder tree so the filter can produce a sample each clock cycle. Second, you will understand FPGA-based motor control: generating PWM with binary counters, reading quadrature encoder signals to determine position and direction, and creating a PID control loop in hardware. Third, you will be able to explain why FPGAs outperform processors for high-speed deterministic control by describing parallelism, pipelining, and resource mapping. Finally, you will design and verify a 16-bit PWM generator and write a simple testbench to check duty cycle and frequency in simulation. Each objective pairs a Verilog pattern with a verification step so you learn both design and validation.

screens.title: FIR Filter — Mathematical Definition
screens.subtitle: Finite Impulse Response and the weighted-sum formula

narration.text: A Finite Impulse Response filter computes a weighted sum of the current input and a fixed number of previous inputs. The defining equation is y of n equals the sum of b k times x of n minus k, for k from zero to N minus one. This is simply a convolution of the input stream with a finite coefficient set. The practical consequence is that the filter has a fixed, finite memory: only the last N samples matter. On a processor you implement this as a loop computing N multiply-accumulate operations per output. On an FPGA, we can unroll that loop into parallel hardware: a shift register holds the delay line, each tap multiplies in parallel, and an adder tree combines the products. A concrete example: a 16-tap low-pass filter with 16-bit inputs and 16-bit coefficients produces 32-bit products and a 32-bit accumulator. A common misconception is that FPGAs somehow change the math — they don't. The FPGA implements the same weighted sum, but hardware parallelism and pipelining change performance characteristics: latency exists because of pipeline stages, but throughput can be one sample per clock. Reflect: how would a 100-tap filter change your choice of fixed-point widths and test vectors?

keyIdea.title: FIR Definition
keyIdea.text: y[n] is a finite weighted sum of current and past inputs; hardware maps the sum to parallel multiplies and an adder tree for throughput.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › FIR Definition
Formal Definition
y[n] = b[0]*x[n] + b[1]*x[n-1] + ... + b[N-1]*x[n-(N-1)]
Key points: finite memory N, coefficients b[k], linear convolution. The filter is linear and time-invariant for fixed coefficients.
Example
A 16-tap low-pass with 16-bit coefficients multiplies each of 16 delayed samples and sums them, yielding a 32-bit accumulator to avoid overflow.
Common misconception
Unrolling the loop does not change correctness: it only changes latency and throughput characteristics; careful fixed-point scaling is still required.
Concrete Design Elements
  • Delay line: shift register holding last N samples.
  • Parallel multipliers: one per tap, ideally mapped to DSP blocks.
  • Adder tree: reduces N products to a single sum with pipeline stages.
Key Takeaway

An FPGA implements the same FIR math but can produce a new output every clock cycle when multipliers and adders are instantiated in parallel and pipelined.

screens.title: Implementing an FIR in Verilog
screens.subtitle: Shift register delay line, parallel multipliers, and adder tree

narration.text: Let's walk through the common Verilog pattern for an FIR filter. The implementation has three parts: a delay line, parallel multipliers, and an adder tree. The delay line is a simple shift register that captures the current sample and shifts previous samples down the line on each clock. Each tap multiplies a delayed sample by a coefficient — on modern FPGAs those multipliers are implemented in DSP blocks by synthesis tools. Finally an adder tree sums the products, often with pipeline registers between stages to maintain a single-sample-per-clock throughput. A concrete code example uses an N-sized reg array for the delay line and a generate block to create the products. A common mistake is to build a wide combinational adder tree without pipeline registers; that will limit clock frequency. Instead, pipeline the adder tree stages so the design meets timing and still yields steady-state throughput. For verification, simulate with an impulse and check that the output matches the expected coefficient sequence. What pipeline stage would you add first if timing fails? Implementing an FIR in Verilog means delay line via shift registers, generate parallel products, then pipeline an adder tree to meet timing while preserving throughput.. In practical terms, shift register delay line, parallel multipliers, and adder tree. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Verilog Pattern
keyIdea.text: Delay line via shift registers, generate parallel products, then pipeline an adder tree to meet timing while preserving throughput.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › FIR in Verilog
Code Walkthrough
// Delay line and product generation (excerpt)
module fir_filter (
  input wire clk,
  input wire signed [15:0] x,
  output reg signed [31:0] y
);
  parameter N = 16;
  reg signed [15:0] delay_line [0:N-1];
  wire signed [31:0] products [0:N-1];
  wire signed [15:0] coeff [0:N-1];

  always @(posedge clk) begin
    delay_line[0] <= x;
    for (integer i = 1; i < N; i = i + 1)
      delay_line[i] <= delay_line[i-1];
  end

  genvar i;
  generate
    for (i = 0; i < N; i = i + 1) begin : mult_gen
      assign products[i] = delay_line[i] * coeff[i];
    end
  endgenerate

  // Adder tree and output register omitted
endmodule
This example shows the delay line and parametric product generation. Synthesis maps the乘 products to DSP blocks when available.
Design Notes
  • Use DSP blocks for each multiplier to save LUTs and achieve higher clock rates.
  • Pipeline the adder tree: add registers between reduction stages to meet timing.
  • Watch bit widths: multiply 16-bit by 16-bit to get 32-bit products and sized accumulator.
Key Takeaway

Unroll the tap loop into parallel hardware, but pipeline the adder tree to keep a high clock rate and one-sample-per-cycle throughput.

screens.title: Mapping Multiplications to DSP Blocks
screens.subtitle: Using DSP resources and MAC pipelines for large filters

narration.text: Modern FPGAs include dedicated DSP blocks containing fast multipliers and optional accumulators. When you write parallel multiplications in Verilog, the synthesis tool will map them to DSP blocks where possible, saving logic fabric and improving speed. For large FIR filters, designers chain DSP blocks into MAC pipelines so each block performs a multiply and a partial accumulate. The process is: first instantiate the parallel multipliers, second organize the partial sums into a staged adder tree, and third add pipeline registers between stages. A 100-tap filter conceptually uses 100 multiplies; the FPGA can implement many of those in parallel across DSP tiles. A common trap is assuming unlimited DSPs: resource constraints mean you may time-multiplex multipliers or use block R A M to store coefficients and iterate across samples for very large filters. For verification, check resource reports after synthesis and run worst-case timing to confirm your pipeline meets the target sample clock. Mapping Multiplications to DSP Blocks means synthesis maps parallel multiplies to dsp blocks; chain blocks into mac pipelines for throughput, but watch dsp resource limits and timing.. In practical terms, using dsp resources and mac pipelines for large filters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: DSP Mapping
keyIdea.text: Synthesis maps parallel multiplies to DSP blocks; chain blocks into MAC pipelines for throughput, but watch DSP resource limits and timing.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › DSP Blocks & MACs
Pipeline Steps
  1. Instantiate parallel multipliers; allow synthesis to use DSP blocks.
  2. Group products into partial sums and create an adder tree.
  3. Insert pipeline registers between adder stages to meet timing.
If DSP resources are limited, time-multiplex multiplications over several cycles and accept lower throughput, or split the filter across clock domains.
Practical Example
A 100-tap filter at 100 MHz aims for one output per clock. An FPGA with adequate DSP tiles can implement most multipliers in parallel; synthesis chains DSP blocks into MAC ladders and registers to form a high-speed pipeline. Verify resource utilization in synthesis reports and adjust design if DSP count is insufficient.
Common Mistake
Forgetting to pipeline the adder tree creates a long combinational path that reduces maximum clock frequency.

screens.title: PWM Generation Basics
screens.subtitle: Counter comparison to create variable duty cycles

narration.text: Pulse Width Modulation is a simple and powerful technique to encode analog levels into a digital pulse stream by changing the fraction of time the signal is high. The FPGA pattern is straightforward: a free-running counter increments each clock cycle, and the PWM output is high when the counter is less than a duty register. With a 16-bit counter you have 65,536 resolution levels. Frequency is clk divided by counter modulus — for a 50 MHz clock and a 16-bit counter, the PWM frequency is about 762 hertz. In practice you choose counter size and clock frequency to trade resolution versus frequency. A common misunderstanding is to assume higher resolution always helps; higher resolution reduces step size but lowers PWM frequency for a fixed clock. Concrete design advice: if you need higher PWM frequency, reduce the counter width or run the PWM logic in a faster clock domain. Verify by simulating the counter wrap and measuring duty high time versus expected duty value. Ask yourself: what happens to LED brightness perception as PWM frequency drops below a few hundred hertz?

keyIdea.title: PWM Pattern
keyIdea.text: A counter compared to a duty register produces PWM. Resolution and frequency trade off via counter size and clock rate.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › PWM Basics
Verilog Pattern
module pwm_generator (
  input wire clk,
  input wire [15:0] duty_cycle,
  output reg pwm_out
);
  reg [15:0] counter;
  always @(posedge clk) begin
    counter <= counter + 1'b1;
    pwm_out <= (counter < duty_cycle);
  end
endmodule
This produces duty resolution of 16 bits. Frequency equals clk / 65536.
Design Trade-offs
  • Higher resolution increases step fidelity but lowers PWM frequency for fixed clock.
  • For visible LEDs, maintain frequency above human flicker; for motors, choose frequency to minimize audible noise and ensure smooth torque.
  • Use clock domain crossing carefully if driving external timers or peripherals at different clocks.
Key Takeaway

PWM is simple to implement in hardware; choose counter width and clock to match the resolution and frequency your system needs.

screens.title: Quadrature Encoder Decoding
screens.subtitle: Counting pulses and determining direction from phase-shifted signals

narration.text: Quadrature encoders provide two signals, A and B, that are 90 degrees out of phase. The FPGA monitors edges and determines direction from the phase relationship: when A leads B the shaft turns one way, and when B leads A it turns the other way. A simple implementation latches previous A and B states, detects rising edges, and increments or decrements a position counter accordingly. The approach is lightweight and deterministic: every relevant edge can be serviced in hardware with no jitter. One concrete example from the chapter shows detecting an A rising edge and examining B to decide whether to increment or decrement. A common pitfall is metastability when encoder signals cross asynchronous clock domains; use double-flops or synchronize signals before edge detection. Also consider pulse rates: high-speed encoders may require debouncing or sampling strategies. For practice, simulate alternating A/B waveforms and confirm the counter increments and decrements as expected. Quadrature Encoder Decoding means detect edges and phase of a and b signals to update a signed position counter deterministically. synchronize inputs to avoid metastability.. In practical terms, counting pulses and determining direction from phase-shifted signals. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Quadrature Decoding
keyIdea.text: Detect edges and phase of A and B signals to update a signed position counter deterministically. Synchronize inputs to avoid metastability.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › Encoder Decoding
Verilog Snippet
module quadrature_decoder (
  input wire clk,
  input wire a,
  input wire b,
  output reg signed [31:0] position
);
  reg a_prev, b_prev;
  wire a_rising = a && !a_prev;

  always @(posedge clk) begin
    a_prev <= a;
    b_prev <= b;
    if (a_rising) begin
      if (b)
        position <= position + 1;
      else
        position <= position - 1;
    end
  end
endmodule
This example updates position on A rising edges and uses B to determine direction. Synchronize 'a' and 'b' into the 'clk' domain before this logic.
Design Notes
  • Use double-register synchronization for asynchronous inputs.
  • Decide whether to count on both edges for higher resolution.
  • Test with synthetic A/B waveforms at worst-case encoder speed to confirm no missed edges.
Common Mistake
Failing to synchronize encoder signals can cause metastability and incorrect counts.

screens.title: PID Controller in Hardware
screens.subtitle: Error, integral, derivative and mapping to FPGA resources

narration.text: A PID controller computes a control output from proportional, integral, and derivative terms applied to the error between a setpoint and a measured value. The three components are computed as error times Kp, the accumulated integral times Ki, and the derivative times Kd. In hardware, you implement error as a simple subtract, the integral as an accumulator updated each control cycle, and the derivative as a difference between successive errors. Multiplications by Kp, Ki, and Kd can be performed by DSP blocks, or by shifts and adds if the gains are powers of two. Running the PID loop at hardware clock rates yields much faster response than a software loop. A misconception is to ignore numeric range: integral accumulation must be bounded to avoid overflow, and derivative computation amplifies noise unless filtered. Verify by applying a setpoint step and observing overshoot, settling, and steady-state error. How would you limit integral windup in hardware? PID Controller in Hardware means compute error, integral, and derivative each cycle; use dsp blocks for multiplies and guard accumulators against overflow and windup.. In practical terms, error, integral, derivative and mapping to fpga resources. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Hardware PID
keyIdea.text: Compute error, integral, and derivative each cycle; use DSP blocks for multiplies and guard accumulators against overflow and windup.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › PID in Hardware
PID Equations (conceptual)
error = setpoint - measured
integral = integral + error * dt
derivative = (error - previous_error) / dt
output = Kp*error + Ki*integral + Kd*derivative
Implement multiplies with DSPs or shift/adds; run this loop every control tick in hardware for deterministic timing.
Practical Considerations
  • Limit integral to prevent windup; implement clamping logic in the accumulator.
  • Filter derivative input to reduce high-frequency noise amplification.
  • Select dt consistently with control loop clock; use fixed-point scaling with headroom.
Key Takeaway

A hardware PID gives fast, deterministic updates. Protect accumulators, manage fixed-point math, and filter derivatives to maintain stability.

screens.title: Verification: Testbenches and Simulation
screens.subtitle: Impulse, step, and waveform-driven tests for filters and control blocks

narration.text: Verification is essential before synthesis. For FIR filters, standard tests include the impulse response and the step response: an impulse should reproduce the filter coefficients in the output sequence; a step verifies DC gain and settling. For PWM and encoder blocks, inject synthetic waveforms in the testbench: toggle duty registers and verify high-time matches expected duty; feed A/B waveforms at the encoder's maximum expected frequency and check counts and direction. For PID loops, subject the controller to setpoint steps and observe overshoot and settling. The chapter suggests using ModelSim for simulation, but the general approach applies to any HDL simulator. A common verification mistake is to test only at low speeds — include worst-case timing and noisy inputs. Always add assertions for invariants like accumulator bounds or that PWM frequency remains stable. After passing functional tests, inspect synthesis reports for resource usage and timing to close the loop between functionality and performance. Verification: Testbenches and Simulation means combine functional tests (impulse, step, waveform) with assertions and worst-case speed checks to verify correctness and timing before hardware testing.. In practical terms, impulse, step, and waveform-driven tests for filters and control blocks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Combine functional tests (impulse, step, waveform) with assertions and worst-case speed checks to verify correctness and timing before hardware testing.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › Verification
Filter Tests
  • Impulse response: output sequence equals coefficients.
  • Step response: check DC gain and settling time.
  • Coefficient sign checks and overflow assertions.
Control & PWM Tests

  • Encoder waveform injection and position verification.
  • PID step tests: measure overshoot, settle, and steady-state error.
Practical Tip
Include assertions in your testbench for range checks and timing invariants. Run worst-case input rates to find timing or synchronization bugs early.

screens.title: System Integration: PWM, ADC, and Processor
screens.subtitle: Using a soft-core to write duty registers from ADC readings

narration.text: A common hands-on system ties FPGA PWM to an LED and uses a processor to update duty values from an ADC. The chapter's activity describes a 16-bit PWM driven by a NIOS II processor reading an ADC on a MAX 10 board. The architecture pattern is: ADC samples the potentiometer, the processor reads the ADC value via memory-mapped input and output, scales it to 16 bits, and writes it into the PWM duty register implemented in hardware. This hybrid approach leverages software for non-time-critical tasks like scaling and user interface, while the hardware PWM guarantees deterministic waveform timing. When designing this integration, ensure the register interface includes proper handshaking or atomic writes if the PWM logic samples duty asynchronously. A misconception is to let the processor update the duty register without synchronization — use double-buffering or write-on-clock-edge semantics to avoid glitches. For verification, simulate register writes and observe that duty changes reflect smoothly when the ADC value changes. System Integration: PWM, ADC, and Processor means use a processor for non-real-time tasks and let fpga hardware produce deterministic pwm timing; synchronize register updates to avoid glitches.. In practical terms, using a soft-core to write duty registers from adc readings. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Hybrid Integration
keyIdea.text: Use a processor for non-real-time tasks and let FPGA hardware produce deterministic PWM timing; synchronize register updates to avoid glitches.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › System Integration
Integration Flow
  1. ADC samples potentiometer and stores result in a register accessible to the processor.
  2. Processor reads ADC value, scales to PWM range, writes duty to PWM register.
  3. PWM hardware uses duty register to produce deterministic output to LED or motor driver.
Implementation Notes
  • Use atomic register write or double-buffering to avoid transient PWM glitches.
  • Keep processor updates at a lower rate than PWM to reduce bus traffic.
  • Verify end-to-end behavior on-board by changing the potentiometer and observing LED brightness.
Key Takeaway

Combine software for flexible control with hardware for precise timing. Synchronize register updates to keep outputs glitch-free.

screens.title: FPGA vs Microcontroller for High-Speed Tasks
screens.subtitle: Throughput, determinism, and parallelism trade-offs

narration.text: Comparing FPGAs and microcontrollers clarifies when to choose hardware. FPGAs implement parallel multiply-accumulate pipelines and can produce one filter output per clock after pipeline fill. A microcontroller executes multiply-accumulate instructions sequentially and may need hundreds of cycles for a long FIR. That makes FPGAs superior for high-tap-count filters or control loops requiring microsecond or sub-microsecond latency. Determinism is another major difference: FPGA hardware executes logic with fixed latency each cycle, while software can face interrupts, cache effects, or variable instruction timings. However, microcontrollers are simpler for low-rate tasks and require far less engineering effort. A common misconception is that FPGAs always win — they do not if the workload is small, or development time and resources are limited. For design decisions, estimate required sample rate, calculate cycles needed per sample on a target MCU, and compare against FPGA throughput to make a reasoned choice. FPGA vs Microcontroller for High-Speed Tasks means choose fpgas for very high sample-rate dsp and tight control loops; choose microcontrollers for lower-speed tasks with simpler development needs.. In practical terms, throughput, determinism, and parallelism trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: When to Use FPGA
keyIdea.text: Choose FPGAs for very high sample-rate DSP and tight control loops; choose microcontrollers for lower-speed tasks with simpler development needs.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › FPGA vs MCU
FPGA Strengths
  • Parallelism: many operations at once.
  • Deterministic timing and low-latency responses.
  • High sample-rate DSP and MHz-range control loops.
Microcontroller Strengths
  • Faster development for control logic and UI tasks.
  • Lower cost for simple low-rate tasks.
  • Easier software debugging and toolchains for algorithm tweaks.
Design Question
Estimate operations per sample on the MCU and compare with FPGA sample-per-clock capability. Choose the platform that meets timing and development constraints.

screens.title: Lab: 16-bit PWM with ADC-Controlled Duty
screens.subtitle: Simulate then run on-board LED controlled by a potentiometer

narration.text: This hands-on activity ties together PWM, an ADC, and a processor. Start by designing the 16-bit PWM generator described earlier. Simulate the module in a testbench: drive duty registers with known values and measure high-time. Next, create a simple memory-mapped duty register and connect it to a soft-core or on-board processor. Read the ADC result from the ADC interface, scale it to 16 bits in software, and write the duty register. On hardware, connect the PWM output to an LED and observe brightness change as you turn the potentiometer. Important checks: confirm that duty updates do not cause visible glitches — use double-buffering if needed; verify PWM frequency and duty resolution in simulation before synthesis; and check for C P U load if you poll ADC values excessively. A common mistake is updating duty too often; prefer sampling the ADC at an appropriate rate and smoothing changes for visible stability. What verification steps will you run on your simulation before moving to the board? The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Simulate PWM module, create memory-mapped duty register, connect ADC via processor, verify in simulation, then test on board with LED and potentiometer.

Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › Lab Activity
Simulation Steps
  1. Simulate PWM with boundary duty values (0, mid, max) and measure high-time.
  2. Simulate ADC read/write sequence and duty register update transactions.
  3. Add assertions for duty register width and PWM frequency stability.
On-Board Checks
  • Observe LED brightness versus potentiometer position.
  • Confirm smooth brightness changes; add software smoothing if needed.
  • Measure PWM on an oscilloscope if available to confirm frequency and duty accuracy.
Key Takeaway

Start with thorough simulation, then perform controlled board tests. Synchronize register writes and limit update rates to prevent glitches.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential concepts you should remember. First, an FIR filter is a finite weighted sum implemented with a delay line, parallel multipliers, and an adder tree; pipelining yields one sample per clock. Second, modern FPGAs include DSP blocks optimized for multiply-accumulate operations that synthesis tools will map your multiplies to, enabling MAC pipelines for large filters. Third, PWM generation uses a counter compared to a duty register to produce a duty-controlled waveform; resolution and frequency trade off via counter width and clock rate. Fourth, quadrature encoder decoding uses A and B phase relationships to determine direction and counts, but you must synchronize inputs to avoid metastability. Finally, a hardware PID loop computes proportional, integral, and derivative terms every control tick; manage integral windup and filter derivative noise. These are the building blocks for high-speed, deterministic control and signal processing on FPGAs.

Final Summary
These primitives let you build high-performance filters and control loops. Verify with simulation, watch resource usage, and protect numerical ranges for stable, reliable hardware implementations.

narration.text: To close, keep three compact ideas in mind. First: parallelism is the FPGA's fundamental advantage — it turns per-sample loops into circuits that can produce one result per clock. Second: DSP blocks and MAC pipelines are the practical mechanism for high-tap FIRs; use pipelining in the adder tree to meet clock timing. Third: for motor control, combine deterministic hardware for timing-critical functions like PWM and encoder reading with software for non-real-time tasks; always synchronize cross-domain signals and guard accumulators. These reminders link the math, the hardware building blocks, and the verification practices that make reliable, high-speed FPGA systems possible. What to Remember means parallel implementation, dsp mapping with pipelining, and synchronized hybrid integration are the cornerstones of fpga dsp and control.. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
